opus-5.5.text:
I think people use "AGI" very loosely, and it hides an important distinction. Human-level intelligence means you can do the things humans can do: pass our exams, hold our jobs, solve the problems we care about. That's a very specific, very narrow slice of the space of possible minds. We just happen to live in it, so it feels general to us.

Truly universal general intelligence would be something that can learn and perform in any domain, including domains humans can't even perceive. Think about it: there are patterns in high-dimensional data, in protein folding, in markets, that we simply cannot see. Our brains evolved to track predators and social relationships on the savannah. A cat, for example, is generally intelligent within its environment, but there's a whole universe of problems it can't even represent. We're in the same position relative to a superintelligent system. We think we're general because we can't see our own blind spots.

So my test would be: is there a problem that's solvable in principle that this system cannot learn to solve? If a human can't do it, we don't call that a failure of general intelligence, we call it "impossible" or "not interesting." But that's anthropocentric bias. A universal intelligence would not have those gaps, or at least would have far fewer.

And this matters for safety. Once you get to human-level, you're very close to superhuman, because the system can copy itself, run faster, and access more memory than any of us. Human-level is not a stable resting point. It's a brief moment on the way to something we fundamentally won't be able to understand, predict, or control. That's what worries me.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes human-level ability from universal intelligence by saying the latter can learn and perform in domains humans cannot perceive, and asks whether it can learn any solvable problem humans cannot.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think the terminology matters a lot here, and people conflate them constantly. Human-level intelligence is really a benchmark tied to one specific species. It's the set of capabilities that happened to evolve in us because they were useful on the African savanna: language, social reasoning, tool use, a certain amount of mathematics, mostly recent. It's a point in the space of possible minds, not the whole space.

AGI, artificial general intelligence, I define as a system that can learn any task a human can learn, at roughly the same level, in roughly the same domains. So it's still anchored to us. It's a kind of substrate-independent human.

Universal intelligence is a much stronger claim. That's an agent that can perform well across all computable environments, in the sense that Legg and Hutter formalized it. It's not limited to problems that happen to be interesting or tractable for humans. There are problems we can't even state. There are patterns in data we are cognitively incapable of noticing, the way a dog can't learn calculus no matter how patient the teacher is. A universal intelligence wouldn't have that ceiling, or at least its ceiling would be set by physics and computation, not by the particular wiring of a primate brain.

And the reason the distinction matters for safety is this. People hear "human-level" and they picture a very smart colleague. Something you can argue with, negotiate with, maybe out-vote. But the moment you have a system that is general in the strong sense, it doesn't stop at human level. There's nothing special about that point. It's a milestone it passes on the way somewhere else, and it likely passes it very quickly, because a system that can do AI research can improve itself. So the gap between "roughly human" and "incomprehensible to humans" might be months, or weeks, not centuries.

So when I'm asked whether we can control human-level AI, my answer is that it's almost the wrong question. We'd be controlling it for a very short period, if at all. The real object we need to reason about is the universal case, and for that one I have yet to see a convincing argument that control is even possible in principle, not just in practice.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes universal intelligence by saying it can handle computable environments and problems beyond human cognitive limits, including things humans cannot state or notice.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish them by the range of problems they can solve. Human-level intelligence is a particular point of comparison: can a system do the kinds of cognitive tasks humans do? That’s a very broad set, but humans also have limitations. We have limited memory, limited attention, and concepts we struggle to understand.

Universal general intelligence is a much stronger idea. You’re asking whether a system can learn and perform across arbitrary domains, including domains humans cannot understand or even recognize as problems. Matching us doesn’t establish that.

And if you mean literally universal—able to solve every possible problem—then there are fundamental computational limits. Some problems are undecidable. So I would be careful to distinguish broad, adaptable intelligence from an intelligence with no limitations whatsoever.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes universal intelligence by its ability to learn and perform across domains humans cannot understand, beyond merely matching human capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human-level intelligence is a very specific point in a much larger space of possible intelligences. We tend to use ourselves as the benchmark because that’s what we know. But humans are good at some things and terrible at others. We have limited memory, limited attention, and all sorts of cognitive biases.

So if you build a system that can do everything a human can do, you’ve achieved something remarkable, but you haven’t necessarily achieved universal intelligence. A more universal intelligence would be able to learn and operate across a much broader range of environments and problems, including ones humans can’t understand.

And even there, you have to be careful with the word “universal.” It doesn’t mean omniscient. There are computational limits, undecidable problems, limits imposed by physics. No intelligence gets to escape those simply by being smarter. So I would distinguish matching the range of human abilities from having a general capacity to adapt across possible domains. Human intelligence is one example of that capacity, not necessarily its upper bound.

r001.rationale: The response says universal intelligence could learn and operate across broader domains, including ones humans cannot understand. It does not clearly state that it can learn skills humans cannot learn.
